ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: the circuit in the attached figure is a BJT bias circuit. The base is directly connected to the positive terminal of the 2 V power supply on the left, and the negative terminal of the left power supply is connected to common ground; the emitter is connected to ground through a 1 kΩ resistor; the collector is connected through a 10 kΩ resistor to the positive terminal of the +10 V power supply on the right, and the negative terminal of the right power supply is also connected to ground. Then reason: the problem gives that β is very large and V_BE=0.7 V. First assume that the transistor operates in the active region. Since the base is 2 V, if the BE junction is forward conducting, then the emitter voltage is V_E=2-0.7=1.3 V. The emitter current is I_E=1.3 V / 1 kΩ = 1.3 mA. When β is very large, I_C≈I_E≈1.3 mA. Thus the voltage drop across the 10 kΩ collector resistor is 1.3 mA × 10 kΩ = 13 V, so the collector voltage would be calculated as V_C=10-13=-3 V. This result makes the collector voltage far lower than the base voltage 2 V, so the collector junction cannot possibly remain reverse biased, and the active-region assumption does not hold. Since the BE junction is already forward biased, while the active region cannot be maintained, the BJT enters the saturation region.

The collector resistor drop would be 1.3 mA × 10 kΩ = 13 V, giving V_C = 10 - 13 = -3 V. This makes V_C far below the base voltage, so the collector-base junction cannot be reverse biased. Since the base-emitter junction is forward biased but active operation is impossible, conclude the BJT is in saturation.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: note the 2 V base bias, the 1 kΩ emitter resistor to ground, and the 10 kΩ collector resistor to the 10 V supply.
